overview:
The idea came out of a quarrel over a prize. At the 1938 Venice Mostra, the world's first international film festival, the awards had been steered toward German and Italian entries under pressure from the two fascist governments, and a group of French officials — the diplomat Philippe Erlanger, backed by education minister Jean Zay — resolved to build a rival event on the French coast where, as they put it, art would not be arranged by political manoeuvring. Biarritz was announced first, in May 1939, but Cannes outbid it with a larger municipal contribution, and on 31 May 1939 the town and the French government signed the agreement that created an International Film Festival. It was to open on 1 September 1939 at the Municipal Casino. That was the morning German troops crossed into Poland; France declared war two days later, and the festival dissolved before it had properly begun, leaving behind little more than a guest list, a shortlist that included The Wizard of Oz, and one private promotional screening.

The revival seven years later was an act of improvisation in a country with very little to spare. Erlanger took the plan up again in 1945; state money was not available, so the funds were raised by public subscription, and the festival finally opened on 20 September 1946 in the same old casino, running into early October. Between eighteen and twenty-one countries took part, depending on which count one follows, and the jury was assembled on the same principle — roughly one member per participating nation, chaired by the historian Georges Huisman. The programming had the texture of the moment: most of the films were about the war that had just ended. Roberto Rossellini's Rome, Open City, David Lean's Brief Encounter, Billy Wilder's The Lost Weekend, René Clément's La Bataille du rail and the Mexican María Candelaria all screened, and rather than name a single winner the jury handed the Grand Prix to eleven films at once, one for very nearly every country in competition. Ray Milland and Michèle Morgan took the acting prizes and Clément the directing award.

Practically, it was a shambles. A storm tore the canvas roof off the venue the day before the results were announced, reels of Hitchcock's Notorious were shown in the wrong order, and the accommodation and transport of a Riviera still recovering from occupation strained under the crowd. None of that mattered much. The town got the tourists it had gambled its subsidy on, and the diplomatic arithmetic of a prize for nearly everyone gave a festival born in anti-fascist protest an opening gesture of reconciliation. The event was not yet annual or secure — money problems cancelled the editions of 1948 and 1950 — and the Palme d'Or, the emblem most people now associate with Cannes, did not exist until 1955.
significance: Cannes established the template that international film festivals still follow: a competitive selection judged by a jury, organised by nation but claiming to answer to art rather than to states, held in a resort town that treats cinema as both culture and commerce. Because it was conceived explicitly as a counterweight to a festival captured by fascist governments, it embedded from the start the notion that where a film is shown and honoured is itself a political question — an argument that has recurred at Cannes ever since, from the shutdown of the 1968 edition to repeated diplomatic rows over selections. The addition of the Marché du Film in the late 1950s turned the festival into the world's main marketplace for film rights as well as its most watched prize, so that a decision made in a bomb-damaged casino in 1946 still shapes which films from outside Hollywood reach a global audience.
coverage: The dataset holds no events beneath this story, so this is written entirely from the festival's own institutional history, the city of Cannes's archive pages, and encyclopaedic accounts, all of which are retrospective and to some degree celebratory. Basic facts are genuinely unsettled even in those: sources give the 1946 closing date as either 5 or 15 October and the number of participating countries as eighteen, nineteen or twenty-one, and the internal politics of the jury's decision to split the Grand Prix eleven ways is not documented in anything I could retrieve.
